utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kvocka. Please be seated and make yourself --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kvocka, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving the false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, as I ask all witnesses, and I have to remind myself, actually, to speak slowly so that everything can be recorded and interpreted. And we should also pause between questions and answers. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown in e-court 1D9688.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the screen before you on the left-hand side, you can see the Serb version. Do you see that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED: [Interpretation] Could the last page please be shown so the witness could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team or are there some inaccuracies there that should be corrected?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is nothing to be corrected. Everything was recorded as I had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same as those put to you by my Defence team, would your answers basically be the same like those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, the essence would certainly be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this statement into evidence according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language a brief summary of Mr. Miroslav Kvocka's testimony. [In English] Miroslav Kvocka started working as a policeman in Omarska in 1981, and he performed the duty of patrol sector leader. When the MUP was divided at the level of BH, the Muslim policemen left the Omarska police squad. The Muslim population had his own army, which was called the Green Berets. The Serbs took over the power in Prijedor on 30th of April, 1992. Several days after the take-over, barricades and check-points started appearing, so that the Serbs had restricted or no access to the Muslim villages and vice versa. In addition, check-points were also established by the military and civilian police, which were ethnically mixed. There were incidents at the check-point in the Muslim village of Hambarine, where several JNA soldiers were killed and wounded. Since the leadership in Hambarine refused to hand over the persons responsible, the army and the police launched combat operation which lasted for a couple of days. Several days later, another ultimatum was leveled against Kozarac, when the armed formations in the village were called on to surrender their weapons. Since the Muslim leadership refused to comply, a military operation ensued. Mr. Kvocka first arrived at the Omarska collect and investigation centre in the last days of May 1992. The duty of the policemen at the Omarska camp was to prevent detainees from escaping or being attacked by third persons. The detainees were not threatened from the inside and the guards would -- and must not physically -- and the guards would and must not physically attack a detained -- detained persons. Zeljko Mejakic, the police squad commander, issued specific instructions not to mistreat detainees and to have as little contact with them as possible. A certain number of disciplinary measures were taken against individuals belonging to Mr. Kvocka's police station. Nonetheless, if any of the guards participated in the incidents, this was hidden especially from Mejakic. Omarska was not surrounded by any wire or fence and the terrain around it was not mined. Two or three days after the work at the Omarska camp began, food started being distributed to the prisoners on a daily basis. There were occasions when Mr. Kvocka himself brought cars full of sandwiches which he would publicly distribute to the detainees. No one ever started any kind of procedure against him for distributing food, nor was he forbidden to help the Muslims by the authorities. On 30th of May, 1992, new buses with detainees arrived at the Omarska camp. In the camp, there were altogether between 15 and 18 women who were considered detainees. Their accommodation and living conditions were better and they were allowed to work in the kitchen. Also, some people of the Serb ethnicity accused for arms smuggling were detained at the Omarska. During the first period of existence of the Omarska camp, several members of the special police from Banja Luka were there. There were problems with the unit because they roamed around the centre and there was talk of them mistreating people and seizing money and jewelry. Mejakic would not issue any order to the leader of this group, but managed to remove the unit from Omarska in mid-June 1992. After they left, the situation in the centre improved drastically. All the detainees were questioned by investigators in order to establish who had participated in the armed rebellion or in its organisation, armament, and financing. The investigators could not issue order to Mejakic, nor could they receive orders from him. Sometimes, investigators could raise their voices during the interrogation, but Mr. Kvocka never saw force being used against the people who were being questioned. The detention would end when the investigation was completed and the suspect cleared of all charges. Mr. Kvocka never assisted to a single murder at the Omarska camp, although he heard rumours that some of the detainees were mistreated. When he had just arrived at the centre, he saw three or four bodies of prisoners who were shot while trying to escape. Furthermore, he was present when, on 31st of May, 1992, a man managed to enter the centre and opened fire on the detainees getting off a bus, in an attempt to vindicate his brother killed by the Muslims. Mr. Kvocka tried to protect his Muslim acquaintances and his wife's brothers. And that is summary of the statement of Mr. Kvocka. At that moment, I do not have additional questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kvocka, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing; that is, through your written witness statement. Now, you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, is that a copy of the B/C/S statement that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've come here to testify about your role in the operation of the Omarska camp in 1992. In that regard, you were tried and convicted in 2001 by a Trial Chamber in this Tribunal of crimes committed in 1992 against non-Serbs in the Omarska camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what is written in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were convicted of crimes against humanity in violations of the laws or customs of war and sentenced to a term of imprisonment of seven years; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Specifically, you were found guilty of count 1, persecution for burden, torture, and beating, sexual assault and rape, harassment, humiliation and psychological abuse, and confinement in conditions as a crime against humanity; count 5, murder as a violation of the laws and customs of war; and count 9, torture as a violation of the laws and customs of war; correct? That was the Trial Chamber's finding.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. Except that I think that during the appeal I think that some of these counts were overruled, I think. It's been a long time. But there weren't any sexual crimes while I was there at the detention centre, and then there were some murders that were also no longer there. That is how I seem to remember the appeals judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, on appeal the Appeals Chamber reversed your convictions in two respects. Regarding two of the four murders you were convicted of and regarding the rape and sexual assault conviction, they said that there was no evidence in that regard in relation to linking it to you, but affirmed your sentence of seven years. That's your recollection of the Appeals Chamber's judgement, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. That's what was stated, that the sentence itself was not affected by the fact that those crimes were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 372 that you participated in the operation of the camp as the functional equivalent of a deputy commander of the guards service and that you had some degree of authority over the guards, yes? That was the finding of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That is what is written in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were interviewed by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 24th and 25th of June, 1998. Do you stand by the answers you gave during that interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, if they were all faithfully transmitted and properly translated, understood. I think that most of it was. There were a few things that were unclear, though, and that was discussed during my trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before we get into the substance of your witness statement, I just want to clarify a matter. And if you can turn to paragraph 9 of your statement, that's now Exhibit P4219, you said that after a change in authorities in Prijedor, Drljaca, the head of the uniformed police became chief of the SJB? That's incorrect, isn't it, because Drljaca was not the head of the uniformed police prior to taking over as chief of the Prijedor SJB? That's right, isn't it? He was not the head of the uniformed police prior to becoming the chief of the Prijedor public security station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand the question. Everything is correctly stated here in this paragraph 9, except that perhaps you're reading it in a different way. Simo Drljaca became the head of the police after the change of the authorities in Prijedor, and then there is a comma, and it says that the second in command was then Dusko Jankovic, and Milutin Caje [phoen] was commander of the Prijedor 1 police station. So this paragraph faithfully reflects what was stated and what is correct anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance. The translation of this document is not correct and that is what misled Madam Sutherland. So the translation of the statement is not exactly correct. That paragraph, 9, perhaps it would be a good thing if it were to be read out and if our interpreters were to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic, but I think Mr. Kvocka has already read out what he has -- what he says is in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that -- Mr. Kvocka, you said that Simo Drljaca was chief of Prijedor police station number 1. The commander of Prijedor police station 2 was Zivko Knezevic, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Knezevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he reported to Simo Drljaca, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Probably. It would go without saying but these are higher stances in terms of my job, but according to the rules that's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 38 of your statement, you say that Drljaca issued an order that the Omarska investigation centre, that is, the Omarska camp, was to be secured by members of the Omarska police squad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could have Exhibit P02640, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you've seen this document before, the one that will come up on your screen. It's the order signed by Drljaca dated the 31st of May, 1992. You were shown this document in your trial. And if we could go to the last page, please. You testified that the signatures that we can see on that last page down below the stamp were signatures of the individuals who received this order on behalf of the security services, and that was Djoko Mejakic at number 1 and Dusan Jankovic at number 2; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, these are persons who received this document for Mico and for this mine, iron, ore mine, and then the public security station Srljeko [phoen] received this on behalf of security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This Dusan Jankovic is the same person that you refer to in paragraph 21 of your statement when discussing the start of operations at the Omarska camp. He was the person who ordered you to go there, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you mention being in Omarska at the commencement of operations around the 28th of May. Serb documentation, and that Exhibit D00470, the Banja Luka commission report dated August 1992, refers to detainees being transferred from Keraterm to Omarska camp on the 27th of May, 1992. Do you accept the likelihood that you're a day or two out with your dates as to when you commenced work at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I accept that. I think that when I testified in my own trial, I said that I cannot recall the exact day but that it is around the 28th of August -- no, the 28th of April or a day before that or a day after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: May, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Mejakic was at the camp every day, sometimes absent for a few hours, and would very often spend the night in the centre. That's what you said when you testified at your trial, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, he spent some time there and sometimes I would be there during the night, sometimes during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Sorry, for the most part, we tried to make sure that one of us was there all the time so that we could help resolve possible problems on the basis of our experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 25 of your statement that Mejakic appointed three men to work duty shifts, and that's Mladen Radic, otherwise known as Mladjo; Momcilo Gruban, also known as Cekalija; and Milojica Kos, also known as Krle. And these people were the go-between, for want of a better word, between Mejakic, yourself and the guards on each of these three shifts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, yes, according to the rules that were in force then, there was this so-called duty officer per shift who tried to be there in one room and, well, yes, to be some kind of go-between too - you can put it that way as well - to help see people resolve problems, and that is why people with more experience and a higher rating were sought for that job among the members of the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Mladjo Radic was an active duty policeman, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. With long years of experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And they also, these three, walked around the camp. They didn't have a specific guard post, did they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During the time -- sorry. During the time that you worked at the camp, you estimated that there were approximately 2.500 people in the camp, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. That's what I said then and I believe that's how it was. I mean, the total number of people that went through the camp, because there was constant coming and going. It's a rough figure because there were no precise records that we could consult now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said in your testimony and in your record of interview, that there were approximately 2.500 people in the camp. Now, you also said that there was between 100 and 120 people that were released, and they were the only people to your knowledge that were released apart from one or two odd people that were taken in a van at the end of the day by the interrogators, and they were taken out of the camp. So this figure of 2.500 was the number of people that you say was in the Omarska camp over the duration of the -- at the time that you were there, and that was up until the 23rd of June; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You saw two very large groups of people brought to the camp on buses, yes? In -- in two different -- two different large groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was present when people were brought in at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The very early days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the first group was the first time you went to the camp after being ordered by Jankovic to go to camp, and then the second large group was in the afternoon of the day Prijedor town was attacked on the 30th of May and also possibly the following day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And detainees were brought to the camp on city buses or intercity buses from Autotransport Prijedor for the most part, weren't they? I mean, most of the buses were from Autotransport Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only forwarding company, the only passenger transport company that existed in Prijedor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Persons escorting the buses were both from the military and the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there was an escort provided by both the military police and the so-called civilian police, the town police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 64 of your statement, you said that you witnessed detainees being made to pass through a gauntlet of military police when they were taken from the buses and they were forced to sing songs and slap each other, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That happened once, when a group was brought.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It was not a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you also witnessed with this group the detainees being beaten by the police and other escorts, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that happened. That's what I was about to say. When people were brought in who had been captured in the forest, there was a group of two or three policemen, and as these people were getting out, the policemen forced them to slap each other. It lasted about 20, 30 seconds until they got in. It was very close to the building, so that gauntlet could not be more than 2 or 3 metres. These people had been caught in the forests at Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also witnessed one incident where four or five people were brought in, and these people were actually brought from the Prijedor SUP, the Prijedor police station. And the policemen who accepted these persons were very rough in conducting the search. You witnessed the police kicking with their feet and hitting with an arm and slapping these persons, and one of these persons was Nusret Sivac, you recall that don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Nusret Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you remember when he was brought into the camp, that he -- the -- the -- the guards that accepted these people were kicking them with their feet and hitting with their arms and slapping these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, you've reminded me. And it's in my statement, that several people were brought in. I remember Nusret Sivac because he had also been a member of the interior. And perhaps out of some feelings of revolt against him, somebody wanted to beat him and kick him, and I tried to protect him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you say that your wife's brothers, Rizak, Nedzad, and Adnan Crnalic, you say you saw them when they were brought to the camp in the afternoon of 31st of May, 1992. And in paragraph 67 of your statement, you say that you took them aside and some ten minutes later got them into an official vehicle and drove them to your family home in the village of Omarska. We are talking here about the family house of your parents in the centre of Omarska, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's Adnan, Rizak, and Nedzad Crnalic. It is misspelled here. They were brought in, but I immediately took them out and drove them to my family home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, they were brought there -- they were brought there en masse in buses with a large number of other non-Serb civilians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. It was that day when the attack happened and that evening, the evening of the day of the attack on Prijedor, two or three buses arrived, and in one of the buses they were too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you omitted to say in your statement why you took them out of the camp. You took them out because you were concerned for their welfare, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It was a semiconscious act. I separated them --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I'm sorry to interrupt you. My question is simply you were concerned for their welfare, yes? I don't want a more lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Correct. Right. But we can discuss in what terms I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. You -- you could tell already at that early stage that the conditions under which the prisoners were housed were bad; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I can say the conditions were not good, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, when you were interviewed by the OTP, do you recall saying that when you were asked to give some concrete examples about the bad conditions, when you were discussing this, you said that the rooms were too small for the number of people, there was no bedding for the detainees to lie on, that there were more people than the capacity of the toilets, and that there were queues and blockages. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps some of these words are not exact. I don't remember saying anything about queues and blockages, but I said that conditions were not great because there were more people than space allowed. There were fewer toilet facilities than necessary for that number of people, the access to water was a bit difficult; meaning, that one had to wait a while to get water. That's what I meant. In any case, the conditions were not commendable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were also concerned that something bad would happen to them due to incidents that had already occurred in the camp, and you supposed that something similar may happen to them, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. And it was my moral duty, if I can't protect everyone and do something for everyone, to do at least something for them. But I did not spare them from the interrogation and some investigative procedures. They were not spared from that. They were just taken to be in my family home where they would feel a little better. In view of the food shortages, they didn't live so well at my home either but it was a little better, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, just in relation to that, you said that they weren't spared interrogation, but isn't it right that you actually selected people to interrogate them that you thought would treat them well? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't specially select any people to interrogate them. I just noticed that these people were available, free, and I knew them from earlier in the service. When you are doing something, you try to choose somebody you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 71 of your statement, you say that Dusan Jankovic ordered you to return your three brother-in-laws to Omarska camp, and that Jankovic told you that you were no longer to work at the camp and that you had to go and work at the Jukovi police station, yes? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that, also in paragraph 71, that when you took them back to the camp, you found Gruban and asked him -- Gruban being Momcilo Gruban, one of the shift leaders or duty officers, as you like to call them, and you asked him to take care of them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In fact, the three men were put in the area known as the glass house on the ground floor of the administration building, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And during your interview with the OTP when you were asked whether you had asked for them to be put into the glass house, you replied that you didn't know what you said exactly but that you told Gruban and also Milica Kos to look after them. You said that you knew that you were leaving the centre, as you called it, so you just asked them to look after them and that "we'd know what that means." Do you recall saying that in your interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that, but I don't remember this particular sentence. I recall, however, that I did ask these people to keep an eye on them, to look after them a little, which is only human, and it's probably they who chose to place them there because that's where they could more easily keep an eye on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, it was your impression that the glass house was the safest room and the one with the best conditions, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Perhaps there were not so many people there, but it was a small space. But the main thing was that it was visible. It was always in the field of vision. It was constantly supervised. So from the point of view of supervision, you could say that people were safer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you didn't want them to be physically assaulted or, worses, to die from horrific beatings which were being inflicted upon detainees, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't want anyone to be physically assaulted, and I dedicated my entire work there to that end. And I even had several clashes with some policemen about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you testified at your trial, you said that when you were asked -- when you asked them to keep an eye on your brother-in-laws so that something stupid wouldn't happen, and when you were asked to elaborate on what this meant, you said, Well, it could be beatings. It could even be killings. And you testified that you had heard that there were guards who were inclined to beat and that this was your source of concern. Do you recall saying that when you testified?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's exactly what I said a moment ago. I had several clashes with policemen, the newly inducted reserve policemen who did not really like me that much because I wanted that work to be done professionally, and such policemen - and there were two or three of them - they had a grudge against me. And it was only logical for me to assume that they could take their revenge on my relatives and other people whom I wholeheartedly tried to help, and I had verbal clashes with these men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in paragraph 57 of your statement you say, "I'm not aware that Zigic entered the centre," and we're talking about the Omarska camp here. As you sit here today, you know full well that he entered the camp and committed heinous crimes against the detainees. You sat through your trial and heard numerous witnesses testifying about crimes committed by Zigic and others who came to the camp with him, and you also knew back then in 1992 when you had to take your three brother-in-laws back to the camp, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That's not right. I did hear a lot during various testimonies here. But while I was at Omarska, and you know that it was only 20 days, including various absences, you know about that from my trial, so actively I worked practically for 12 days. And during that time, I guarantee - and I can repeat now - that Zigic did not come to the camp, and I didn't even hear that he had come to the camp during my absences. You know that I worked there only for a short time, a very little number of days, and during that time Zigic did not visit the camp. But I did hear here at the Tribunal that many people claimed that he did come to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, during that time. I maintain that I never saw him come.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And quibbling over the number of days, I think it was found in your trial that you were there for 17 days, not 12 days - correct? - in total.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. In total. But I mention that I was on sick leave for three days, I also got two days off to deal with some of my problems, so I practically worked less. But I accept 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You -- well, you were there for 17 days, up until the 23rd of June, you worked. Taking off the days that you had off in the early June and in mid-June, that left a total of 17 days, which I think you've now agreed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Correct. That's what the Trial Chamber found, and I accept it. I'm just saying that there were a few days less because when I spent one day off, I would not work the next day at the centre. If you take into account the way the shifts worked, I did not work for three days when I was sick and plus Zeljko gave me two days off to deal with some personal matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: But it's not a problem, let it be 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Detainees were being abused by some of the camp guards and from persons coming in from outside from early on in the operation of the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there were certain incidents. We can recall them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that when you were interviewed, that after a few days -- after incidents involving visitors from outside coming into the camp and abusing the detainees, that after a few days a unit came to help. And there was talk that these were members of the special police from Banja Luka. And that these men came from Banja Luka five to ten days after the operation of the camp. You recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 58, you state that you never saw a single murder. You go on to say that when you arrived at Omarska for the first time, you saw three or four dead bodies. You, in fact, saw these bodies when you returned back to the Omarska camp on that first day in daylight around 8.00 a.m.; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, correct, because the first time I came was by night. You couldn't see anything around that time. And at around 8.00 you took over the guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the only thing you saw were between nine and 12 buses - that's right? - some were full of detainees and others were empty?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that night --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: -- when the prisoners were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. These bodies that you saw, these three to four bodies, were taken away two days later in a small yellow TAM truck; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It was said that an onsite investigation has to be conducted, but the standard, proper onsite investigation was indeed never done, probably because of the overall situation in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 24 of your statement, the last sentence, you say that during your work in the centre, you spent almost half the time in the office and the other half outdoors. But this -- this half-time business was only in relation to the first two days you spent in Omarska, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think, roughly speaking, I spent half of the time in that office upstairs where there were several typists and Zeljko and some other people who were on duty in the same shift and some people who were taking statements and giving them to the typists to type up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: So speaking of the overall, the total time I spent --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- can you just finish your sentence? I'm sorry for interrupting you. You said: "So speaking of the overall, the total time I spent ..." You're saying it's half and half?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Out of those 17 days that I worked, as you said, out of all of it half of the time I was outdoors and half of the time, roughly speaking, in the office. Not only those first two, three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, just let me remind you of what you testified to. You said that you spent 16 to 17 hours in the investigation centre during the first two days, and out of that half the time in the office. Do you recall saying that when you testified?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It's possible that I said that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Those days and all the other days I spent half of the time outdoors, half in the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, for the rest of the time in the camp, you told Mr. Reid in your OTP interview that of the 12-hour shift, you usually spent between one to two hours in the office and around 10 or 11 hours outside. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember saying it so definitely. Even if I did, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I can only --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] When -- when -- when it was put back to you, you said earlier you would be outside for approximately maybe 10 hours of your shift, outside the office. You said: "Yes, one could say that. We don't have to be so precise. Reid says: "No, but approximately, the majority of your shift was spent outside?" And you said: "Yes." Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. One day I would spend more time outdoors, the other day I would spend more time in the office. So overall, it was half/half. I was a lot outdoors. Some days I spent seven or eight hours outdoors. Sometimes there were days when I spent ten hours outdoors and went into the office for only five minutes. Such things also happened. I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that in paragraph 78 of your statement, you say that according to your information there were no more than a total of five deaths in Omarska. I want to clarify that, what you mean by that. You mean no more than five deaths in Omarska during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: This is more or less what I thought. What I knew during my stay there was there were five, six, or perhaps four of them. I can't tell you anything more precisely. I knew that people were saying that one of them died of natural causes. There were four bodies that we found there. I don't know whether during that incident when a soldier opened fire in revenge that two people died. So all in all, that could -- there could have been like five or six bodies all together. This is what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Mehmedalija Nasic, who was shot by Dragan Popovic, also known as Pavelic, on or about the 10th of June, 1992; there was also Becir Medunjanin who was beaten to death by Zoran Zigic and Duco [phoen] Knezevic around mid-June; and there was also, during the time that you were there, around 12 to 14 June, the killing of Emir Ramic, Amir Saric, and Dalija Hrnic. That's just to name a few. So you don't dispute that there were more than five deaths during the time you were there, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I'm saying once again, there may have been another killing, there may have been, but I am telling you what I knew at the time. And as far as the previous paragraph is concerned, I did not mention the case of Nasic who was killed by Popovic, also known as Pavlic, not Pavelic. I heard about that. In the morning when I arrived at work, I heard that an incident had happened during the night. Popovic testified before this Court and I believe that he explained in very great detail as to what had happened that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, of course, there was also those four people that were shot by the -- the person who came into the camp on the 30th of May, and that's Esef Muranovic, Avdo Muranovic, and another gentleman whose name is Tevfik, whose nickname is Sefik. You know about that killing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, perhaps you're talking about those bodies that we found there already dead, perhaps you're talking about those people, or perhaps those who succumbed to their wounds sustained during that incident. Maybe those bodies overlapped. But I didn't know any of their names. I didn't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, these were different people from the three or four bodies that you saw on that first day. Witnesses testified at your trial that on almost a daily basis several dead bodies -- and this is in the judgement of paragraph 86, that several dead bodies would be seen near the white house which would then be loaded onto a yellow TAM or Tamic truck the following day and taken away. And they also found in paragraph 66 of the judgement that dead bodies were left to fester outside for days at a time and a terrible stench and fear pervaded the camp. Now, is it really your evidence that you never saw another dead body lying anywhere within the Omarska camp compound during the 17 days that you were working in the camp, in particular, given that you've told us a moment ago about the amount of time that you spent outside?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, you say it yourself that the witnesses said almost every day which means not every day. So when you take into account my work and my number of days, and that it was every third day that I worked a day shift, it is only logical, and I still claim that what I saw, and I told you honestly what it was, and I've said it several times before this Court, I've told this Court already about those things that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said earlier in your testimony that you and Mr. Mejakic were always making sure that someone was in the camp and that you were -- it's right, isn't it, that you were working 12-hour shifts. Apart from those first couple of days, you then got into a routine where you were working 12-hour shifts each? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Zeljko and I were more experienced than professional policemen, and we agreed of our own initiative to make things function better for the prisoners and that's how we proceeded. We may have been wrong in doing that. We would never have been charged with command responsibility, which is not in the final decision, because it was rejected. However, it was our moral duty to teach reserve police officers to help the prisoners because we didn't have any other duties or obligations. We didn't have any other possibilities or duty or any other authorities or competences. So one can say that it was our agreement in principle, which does not mean that we follow through a hundred per cent. It was our internal agreement that one of the two of us should always be down there, but it did sometimes happen that none of us were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 54 of your statement, you say that you sometimes heard cries from the offices in which the investigations were being conducted. And in paragraph 62, you gave one example of when you were aware of someone being beaten during interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember an event when --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You reported this incident to the -- it's actually outlined in your statement, so you don't need to republic it. You reported this incident to the interrogation co-ordinators, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, my intervention in that case was more about establishing whether any of the police officers were involved in tortures or forcible interrogation, because it did sometimes happen that a policeman would be present in the same office where the investigators were or whether such things were done by the investigators. There was an investigator from Banja Luka who slapped a prisoner on that occasion. There was no need to report the incident to the investigator in such cases. And that was not or obligation, in any case. The investigators were, in a way, superior to us, but -- although they were not in a position to order us. As a rule, investigators are always superior to the policemen, but whether that was always the case or not, that's another issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, do you remember saying in your interview when Mr. Reid said, "Did you complain,..." and this is about this very incident: "Did you complain to the chief of the interrogators?" And you said: "I told them the same thing. I told them. I told them something in the sense why were they allowing it and they should know that it was not right."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree. I don't remember who this person belonged to, which of the services he belonged to. I don't know who I complained to, more specifically. But I agree that I spoke to their boss. However, the meaning of my previous answer is that it was not my official duty to complain, officially. It was enough to report to the superior officer. But I repeat: Those were the rules. It was a conflict between -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, the interrogation co-ordinator's room was at the end of the corridor of the rooms where all the interrogations were taking place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So it's from that room at the end of the -- at the end of the corridor, I think. They would be in a position to be able to hear noises coming from these interrogation rooms, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Relatively. The corridor was long. The office was at the end of the corridor. And the other office was across the corridor from our police officers' office. That's why we noticed. Whether they heard or not is a very relative thing and I can't testify to that. I can only claim that I heard something, I entered the office, I saw a person standing there who was rather red in the face, which means that he had been slapped which was not unheard of in our communist police service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say you saw a person standing there who was rather red in the face, you're talking about one of the detainees, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, if we are talking about this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you then went on to say in paragraph 63 of your statement that: "During my work at Omarska, it seemed to me that there were other instances where force was used." And I want to clarify by what you meant by "other instances of force being used."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That's how it was done. There were talks among the guards about people having been beaten, so, yes, we did receive several pieces information about people having being beaten. But I repeat, it never happened before my eyes. Nothing was ever reported. But one could suspect that some people were beaten at the time while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you testified at -- in your trial that you heard screams when you were in the office. And you said: "I did see men, and in view of the conditions of the situation, they were suffering. But I didn't see how they were suffering. I saw people with injuries." Do you recall saying that, that's right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. This is what I knew from what people were saying among themselves --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: -- or when people were taken out to lunch I looked at their face, and I could see bruises and they had their noses broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and one example of that is that you saw and spoke to people who -- who had visible bruises on their face, and you concluded that they had been beaten up, and in particular, Sefik Terzic, also known as Kiki, the hairdresser; and Rezik Kukanovic [phoen]. You remember seeing them and speaking with them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I saw them. One of them had bruises on his face. Since I knew both of them from before the war, they didn't want to tell me anything. They said, Let's not make things worse. It's fine. It's okay. That was their answer. They didn't want to tell me what had happened to them, as far as I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Gajic from the Omarska medical centre testified in your trial that his diagnosis was that most of the injuries occurred from blows with blunt instruments, "including, for example, an army boot, then the butt of a rifle, hands, and fists." And that's a finding that the Trial Chamber made at paragraph 65 of the judgement. Is -- these are the sort of the injuries that -- that you are saying that -- that you saw visible on the detainees? These type of injuries, caused by these objects, I mean, instruments and boots.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, if that's what the doctor said, I suppose that he was right. I did see a few such cases, but I had to tell you that in my previous statements and in my previous testimonies, I said that I was present when detainees were being brought in, and a lot of them had been injured before they were ever brought to the investigation centre, people were arrested in woods, they had participated in some clashes, and they showed visible injuries. So one cannot say that the detainees were injured only in the investigation centre. Many of them had been injured during combat. And as for those about whom I have testified here, those were the people who were in the investigation centre, who sustained injuries there, and whom I saw personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 44 of your statement that all together there were between 15 and 18 women at Omarska who were considered detainees. In your record of interview, you said that there were approximately 20 to 25 women in the camp. You're aware, are you not, that there were at least 36 women who were detained and who were not free to leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can't give you the exact number. But while I was there, there could not have been over 20. When I left, the numbers could have gone up or down, I can't be sure of that, but while I was there, there were about 20 of them. There may have been 19 or 21, I really cannot be more precise in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that their accommodation and living conditions were better because they were women. You're aware, aren't you, from your trial, that some of these women were raped and sexually assaulted at night by the guards?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I know what I heard during trial. While I was there in the camp, nobody talked about that. Nobody ever complained. There were never rumours about that. Nobody was aware of any --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: -- so I was thinking we were coming back to the trial judgement where it was acknowledged that that's how it was when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But even if you weren't aware of it then, you certainly were aware of it when you made your statement to the Defence, weren't you, that these women had been mistreated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: You know what? I provided a statement about what I know. I can't tell the Defence that I heard about the rapes in Omarska in July and August. I don't think it would be fair on my behalf to say something like that in my statement, because I only heard about that during trial which means that much after my time spent in the investigation centre did I heard about the rapes in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. [In English] transcript. [Interpretation] There have been several mistakes. However, on lines 24 and 25, the witness said: "I could not have stated in my statement to the Defence team what I heard here during the trials."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you confirm having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is exactly what I said. I said that it would not be fair on my behalf to say to the Defence team what I heard during the trial which took place in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraphs 24, 42, and 66 of your statement, you refer to a runway. The runway that you're referring to in your statement is the area also known as the "pista," is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: There is the term "pista," which is an asphalt surface between the two buildings, and very often the detainees were called to go to that runway from their respective buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just so we can orient the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P00543 please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript again. Line 24 seems to be fatal. The witness said -- the witness asked to be let out to go to the runway. The detainees themselves were asking to be let out to go to the "pista," not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is precisely what I said, that they demanded, asked, requested to be allowed to go out, the detainees themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 4 now it says that the witness requested to be allowed to go out. The witness actually said that the detainees requested and demanded to be allowed to go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard. Shall we continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you see a picture of an aerial photograph of the Omarska camp in front of you on the screen. With the usher's assistance, can you use the pointer and just point to this "pista" area or runway as you call it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The area between these two buildings. And now I marked its border with the ring.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're pointing to the -- or you've just drawn a square of the cemented area between the administration building on the left and the hangar building on the right; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then in the foreground, we can see the -- what's known as the white house on the grassed area. And then to the -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Correct. There is a building here. It's facade is white. I know from my trial that it is known as the white house. During my stay in Omarska, that term was not used. The building was not called the white house. It was just one of the buildings within the complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where detainees were housed, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that there were also several people detained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then down towards the right-hand corner at the end of the hangar building, there is the building known as the red house; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, correct. There is a red building there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that we need to keep this marked photograph. It was simply to orient Your Honours, and I've identified for the record the square that -- where the witness marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to tender this. We would kindly ask the witness to place the date and to initial the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if that's going to happen, it can come in as a Prosecution exhibit. I -- I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was trying to save one more exhibit number for you, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- it can be a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you kindly put the date, which is 20th January, 2014, and your signature, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 42 of your statement, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And shall we assign a number for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 42 of your statement, you mentioned that once you noticed that 50 men were lying prostrate. Now you mean that they were lying on their stomachs with their heads down, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now during your 17 days in the camp up until the third week of June 1992, you said when you were interviewed by Mr. Reid that you saw around 3- to 400 people on the "pista"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. I suppose that that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember and I do remember that that's how it was, but I couldn't give the number; 300, 400, 250. In any case, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you were asked how many of them would be there approximately, talking about the "pista," and you responded, "Up to 300 or 400." Now, does that refresh your recollection? Because if it doesn't, we can go to the page, but you may now recall it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I remember that I said something to that effect. I couldn't remember the number that I mentioned, but I remember that more or less that was the number, and I don't see a problem. I accept what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there was also a machine-gun set up on the roof of the administration building in the direction of the "pista" area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case for only one day, not even a whole day. That was the kind of security that was in place, but that was abolished, that was suspended. It was done by somebody who did not even belong to the police. Several people from the Territorial Defence were involved at first when there were not enough police officers, and there was a soldier with a machine-gun because there -- it had been estimated that a guard post was needed to be there. But I claim that it didn't last more than one day and not even a whole day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, witnesses and Mr. Mejakic think that it was there for more than one day. You were asked: "Mr. Reid: Was there a machine-gun set up on the roof of the administration building overlooking the 'pista'?" You said: "It's possible that it was located here on this roof or maybe there was a small terrace there." Mr. Reid said: "On the roof?" You said: "Not absolutely on the roof." He said, Mr. Reid: "But outside overlooking this area here, would that be correct?" And you said: "Yes." Overlooking this area, meaning the "pista" area that you'd just been talking about. Do you recall saying that, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have to intervene, please. The sentence was misinterpreted to the witness. The interpretation he received was: "Absolutely on the roof."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said: "Not absolutely on the roof." Mr. Reid said: "But outside overlooking this area here, meaning the 'pista' area, would that be correct?" And you said: "Yes." Do you recall saying that to Mr. Reid?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: After 15 years, it is really hard to remember word for word what it was that I said to Mr. Reid. The essence was that there was this machine-gun either on the terrace or on the roof for a short period of time, and I cannot remember exactly whether it was on the terrace or on the roof, but they're very close to each other. It's a very small difference in terms of altitude, if you will. So it was there probably because there was a 360-degree view, and the soldier who was probably in charge of external security was supposed to observe the entrance to the investigation centre and to protect it possibly from any kind of incursion. I seem to believe that that is why that machine-gun was so high up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation. I'm not sure that "prilaz" should be interpreted as "ulaz." So it was a question of height, not of the entrances themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can lend assistance to this. Ms. Sutherland, I take it you have more?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was about to say after we had finished with this matter, it would be -- would it be a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue. You're done with this topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I mean, I actually can't -- I don't understand Mr. Karadzic's intervention where he says, "It was question of height, not of the entrances," because what was interpreted in English to me made sense from the witness's answer, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may say, access,"prilaz," entrance here "ulaz." [Interpretation] Entrance is gate and access is the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I assume that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you say that it was put there to observe the access to the investigation centre, or did you say that it was put there to observe the entrance to the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: This is what I said: Probably the machine-gun was put high up so that it could monitor the entire surrounding area around the investigation centre from all sides, where the entrances were, where the surrounding area was, that is why it was so high up. Since it was not referred to whether it was fenced off or not, so probably the idea was that during the first few days someone might try to break into the investigation centre and that is why the idea was to control it from that area. So the entire area. That is why it was so high up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think there was any problem in understanding the general context. We'll have a break, Mr. Kvocka, for half an hour, and resume at 5 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in relation to the water, the Trial Chamber in your case at paragraph 57 said that the detainees were supplied with drinking water but that the quantity of water supplied to the detainees was clearly inadequate.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what the judgement says. I think that there were sufficient quantities, but it was difficult for everybody to get water at the same time. That meant that people would have to wait a bit. That was my understanding of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to accommodation, in paragraph 40 of your statement, you mention that the conditions in the hangar building were quite pleasant. That's what you said, didn't you? You didn't spend any length of time in there, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I went in there only a few times because I had some minor matters to deal with. As for the conditions, well, that could be interpreted in several ways. It wasn't that it was that dirty or that it was altogether inadequate, that the roof was leaking or that it was too hot or something like that. From that point of view, that was all right. But then, on the one hand, there were no beds. So from that point of view one could say that the conditions were not good.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said in your interview that people were -- were housed on the "pista" because -- because the other buildings were full; is that right? You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, possibly people were housed on the "pista," when many people were brought in and before they were all put up. But in due course, they would all end up in doors, not on the "pista." And I think I've already said that during the days when some people were taken out to the "pista," I remember right now that there were some rotations, that sometimes people from the hangar would be taken to the "pista," and then on another day people from another facility so that they would get some fresh air.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Because it was so overcrowded and stifling where they were in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: All right. It may be put that way, since there are several people -- well, of course, there were big windows there and then the windows could be opened in order to air the facilities now overcrowded. Well, I said that it wasn't very bad, but it wasn't extra, extra bad either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said there were two toilet facilities in the hangar building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, two or three toilets were at the entrance into the hangar building. You'd already enter the building and then there is a small corridor and then two or three toilets on one side and two or three toilets on the other side. I think that there were two rooms there as well where detainees were put up. I cannot remember now. I cannot say specifically. But there were at least two --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: -- on either side of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so thousands of detainees had to use these -- these limited toilet facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Everybody probably had to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The detainees were also hosed down on the "pista," yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The detainees? It was once that I saw the detainees washing on the "pista." They were doing it themselves. We don't have the sketch there now, but on the very border-line of that red line that I placed there, there is a system of taps where there was water running nonstop. There were several on both sides. And once, I noticed that they would strip to the waist and wash using that water around the "pista," say around these buildings. There were certainly a few of those hydrants used by firemen, and my impression was that the detainees asked for water to be used from there, too, because I know that during the day the detainees would sit on the grass, those from some of the facilities there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said the sanitary conditions in Omarska were below an acceptable level. That's what you said at your trial, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, all right. As far as normal conditions are concerned, conditions when there would be no conflict or anything like that, that would not be acceptable. But as for this general commotion and everything, it's a matter of assessment, and I would kindly ask that I not be the one to make that assessment. For some they were okay, for others they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also testified that the food given to the detainees was unsatisfactory; the quantity of one meal a day and that the quality of that one meal wasn't good. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It is correct that I spoke about that, that there wasn't enough food. During the first ten days or so, I think there were two meals. And then there was less food. And then in the coming days, I think there was only one meal per day. I don't know how long that went on. I left. There wasn't enough food, generally speaking, and I know that the guards would have to share a single slice of pie because there wasn't enough food for all. Outside Prijedor there was a blockade, so there weren't enough stocks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also know of cases where detainees were too ill or injured from beatings to go to the canteen to take a meal, don't you? You were informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I cannot remember a specific case that somebody could not go to eat. As for the other thing, that there were ill people and injured people, I already spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Maybe it's not too important, but the witness said that the stocks had been exhausted by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in relation to the medical assistance that was provided, your Trial Chamber found at paragraph 63 of the judgement that the assistance that this medical team offered to the thousands of detainees was grossly inadequate. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That is probably a statement made by the Trial Chamber, and I would want to go into that, whether it's correct or not correct. Whether this was sufficient, well, probably, but to a lesser degree in view of the number of detainees, but there was some kind of medical care. I know that medical staff came from the Omarska health centre, and even a doctor from Prijedor, as far as I can remember now. A medical technician came in every day, and he had some medicine. Now, whether that was enough or whether it wasn't enough ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So what was happening in the camp that required a medical -- the doctor. There were illnesses and there was also people that had to be treated from the beatings; true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, there were people who were supposed to be treated. There were people who were ill. There were people who were injured. There were people who were wounded during war operations. There were also those who were injured within the camp during certain incidents that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 27 of your statement, you say that: "With regard to the Geneva Conventions, I acquired some knowledge of them during my police training." This is the first sentence of that paragraph. In fact, you had no training regarding the Geneva Conventions in the police academy nor in any other training you had later on, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It is correct that I did not have any kind of special training in relation to the Geneva Conventions. I had training that was police training, police roles, but I know that too, that it was always stated in the pre-war system that all laws were brought into accordance with the Geneva Conventions. So all the rules that were in force in the police were considered to be in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said that you didn't have any kind of special training. You had no training. Do you recall at the end of your interview with Mr. Reid, he asked you whether there was anything you wished to say, anything you wished to add, and you read from a prepared statement, and you said this, "Forth...," I -- I quote: "Forth, in the police academy," because this was the fourth paragraph that you were reading from, "... in the police academy nor in any other training I had later on, we were not told about anything about the Geneva Conventions. There was no such obligations in the police, that the policemen would know about it, because police functioned in completely different conditions, completely different circumstances that covered by the Geneva Conventions." So this wasn't an answer prompted by any question by Mr. Reid, this was something that you proffered yourself at the conclusion of the interview reading from a prepared statement that you had?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I said the same thing during my previous answer, that I had not undergone any special training regarding the Geneva Conventions, and no policeman in the former system in Yugoslavia did. But as for the legislation that was in force at the time, it was brought into accordance with the Geneva Conventions, so there was no need to have any kind of special training regarding the Geneva Conventions. So it is the same answer that I provided to Mr. Reid and also in response to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now you testified that you believed that the regulations were violated and that also that there were probably violation regarding the conditions of detention.
