And you said that one could see that the conditions were not such as to justify the treatment. Do you recall saying that when you testified?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I probably did. If it is considered that any detainee -- or every detainee during a war or any other conflict should have a bed, then if there is such a rule, then that rule was violated. If they were supposed to have enough food, then probably that kind of rule was violated too, if that is the way you look at it. That is how I looked at it. That is what I thought when I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 28 of your statement that you don't know whether there were decisions made by an investigating judge to extend the detention or release people in Omarska camp. You know, don't you, that the president of the Crisis Staff issued an order forbidding the individual release of detainees from the Trnopolje, Keraterm, and Omarska. And that's part of Exhibit P02915.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I can just say that I know that in the beginning a group of detainees were released after investigation, and then there may have been a few other individual cases when people were released. And then after that, people were not released. Now, whether somebody was released after I had left Omarska, I don't know. As for this order, I don't know about it. If you have it somewhere in your records, then that is the case. But it was never presented to me and I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we kindly ask to have that order shown to the witness? It pertains to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Your Honour. It was -- it's dated the 2nd of July, 1992, and I simply wanted to know whether the witness was aware of whether he had heard about the president of the Crisis Staff issuing this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, the Trial Chamber findings in relation to your knowledge of crimes being committed, they said this: That you undoubtedly knew that a -- this is at paragraph 384 of your judgement, that he undoubtedly knew that a wide variety of crimes were being committed and that physical and mental violence was systematically used to threaten and terrorise the detainees in the camp. And they also said at paragraph 385: The evidence demonstrate that Kvocka had extensive knowledge of the abusive practices, and conditions, and knew that serious crimes were regularly committed in the Omarska camp. And they went further and said in paragraph 397: It is indisputable that he was present while crimes were committed, and he was undoubtedly aware that crimes of extreme physical and mental violence were routinely inflicted upon the non-Serbs imprisoned in Omarska. And despite the knowledge of the abusive treatment and conditions, he continued to work for at least 17 days in the camp where he performed the tasks required of him skillfully, efficiently, and without complaint.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now that's the truth of it, isn't it, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question. Do you mean to say that you have objection to the questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I wonder, I wonder whether this question is a bit too complex, whether the witness could include everything in a brief answer. It could be broken down, this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the witness has difficulty in answering this question. She just summarised the judgement -- of his judgement and then put some questions. Let us see whether the witness can answer the question. Mr. Kvocka, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll try. So this is a citation from the judgement, and I have no comment with regard to that. As for all my knowledge regarding this citation and everything that I did, I talked about that to Mr. Reid for several days and then also I testified before this Court, and there is probably a transcript. And I testified for six or seven days or so. I said in that statement -- and I always said the same thing, it's always one and the same story, and I cannot comment on these conclusions, whether they got it 100 per cent right, all the things that I spoke about, and then, of course, there were other testimonies too, and maybe other people were believed in a different way. I'm just saying that this conclusion, that I did that systematically, wilfully, and so on, that is not correct. As a matter of fact, on one occasion I stated, and that is written somewhere, that I would have done the same thing in terms of the way in which I worked, because it is impossible to present here the effort that I made and the personal dignity that I invested in helping the people who were obtained. That would be it. That is what I can say now briefly about that. You've read the judgement and it is the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in paragraph 32 of your statement, you say that you know that certain number of disciplinary measures were taken against individuals belonging to the Omarska police station. I just want you to tell me the names of these individuals, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I know [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't think we are getting the English translation. Could you start over again, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to this question, I know there were several disciplinary proceedings because some people were removed. They did not come to work for several days. Instead, they went to give statements to the internal police department or some other institution. I don't know exactly. But I know 100 per cent that Mr. Popovic was absent from work six or seven days due to disciplinary proceedings. That's all I can remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kvocka, the person that you just mentioned, Popovic, was the person that murdered Mehmedalija Nasic, and you are saying that he was disciplined by being kept away from the camp for several days. Is that what you're saying? That was the extent of a disciplinary action for a murder?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that I know that he was absent after that incident, and that Zeljko or somebody said that disciplinary proceedings were underway. Now, how they ended, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: -- and whether his punishment was this absence or not, that's not my judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified -- you testified that you never heard or knew of any formal investigation being initiated to find out about any of the things that had happened in the Omarska camp. That's what you said in your testimony, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I never found out the final outcome of any proceedings that may have taken place, because nobody had the obligation to inform me nor did I have the right to inquire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said in paragraph 33 of your statement that you know that two or three guards were dismissed. I just need their names. Can you just tell me the names of the guards that were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I cannot remember now. Perhaps I mentioned some names when I testified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: If I did, you can trust that. And also several people were rotated, several people from the Territorial Defence, and some other units who were there in the early days, but not later. I really can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, no indictments were ever brought by the Serb authorities against persons who committed murders, beatings, sexual assaults against the civilians detained in the Omarska camp, were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I don't know whether they did or didn't. I don't know if there were any trials. I'm really not the right person to ask because I don't work in the criminal investigation service or the prosecutor's office. I am just a regular policeman who doesn't have access to these things, so I don't know either way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to leave the Omarska camp now and move to Keraterm camp. The massacre that occurred on or about the night of the 24th of July, 1992, where at least 150 non-Serbs were killed, that was talked about a lot in Prijedor, wasn't it? You didn't hear anything specific but there was talk among the people about it. That's what you said in your record of interview, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. If I said that at the time, that means I knew it at the time, and now I would say the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now I want to talk about disarming of the non-Serb population. You heard on Radio Prijedor ultimatums by the Serb authorities for non-Serbs to surrender their weapons; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, whether I personally heard it on the radio, I'm not sure. But there were -- there were appeals to surrender weapons --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So there --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: -- when it was already quite certain that there would be a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you didn't hear anything similar in relation to the Serb population; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: -- because I think power had already been taken over. In any case, no, not in our specific area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were never ordered to disarm the Serb population in the village of Omarska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as you said in the area where you lived in in Prijedor, there was no -- no call for the Serbs to hand in their weapons. You --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, no. There were no such appeals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier today about there being clashes and that people were wounded in -- in armed clashes. And paragraph 18 of your statement in relation to the incident at the Hambarine check-point, you said that the police attempted to find a solution and asked for Oliskovic [phoen] to be handed over. And when that didn't happen, a day or two after the incident, clashes occurred in the village. However, when the alleged perpetrators were not handed over by the village of Hambarine, the village was attacked and it was shelled for a day and homes were destroyed. There were no armed clashes, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I don't know how you look at it, but I know there was an incident. I heard about it because I was not involved in that incident. The incident was at Hambarine, a military vehicle was attacked, and I believe one or two soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've talked about that and you said that after that incident, the people were then asked that -- that -- that was the incident, which you said then -- the -- the -- the people of Hambarine were asked to hand over Oliskovic, and when that didn't happen, a day or two after the incident, clashes occurred in the village. What I'm putting to you is there were no clashes, it was simply a military attack. There was shelling for a day. Houses were destroyed. There were no -- there was no armed clashes, fighting, shelling between the Muslims and the Serbs. It was a military attack on the village of Hambarine by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: All I know is that an action was taken by, I think, both the army and the police - I think it was a combined operation - to capture the perpetrators of that attack and arrest them. Now, what was the cause of that clash, of that conflict? I don't know because I was not involved in the event. I know the story was that the population had withdrawn deeper inside towards some sort of settlement, Kurivaj [phoen], I believe, in this hilly area. But what exactly happened, whether we call it attack or clash, or conflict, I really don't know, and I cannot give you evidence about that. All I know was that an operation was undertaken to apprehend the perpetrators who had failed to surrender after an ultimatum was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, in paragraph 19 of your statement, you talk about in relation to Kozarac, you say that there were clashes there. Again, after this incident on the Banja Luka-Prijedor road, what followed was a planned military attack on Kozarac where the village was shelled for two days. And thereafter, the Muslim population were rounded up, the men and the women and the children and the elderly -- the men were separated from the women and the children and the elderly, and the men were taken to the Omarska camp, and the women and the children and the elderly to the Trnopolje. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: You could put it that way. I don't know exactly if they were immediately taken from there to Omarska camp. I believe at the time of the attack on Kozarac, the investigation centre did not even exist. But again, I was not directly involved so I don't know. I know there was a clash, although you will be angry if I use the word "clash." Some sort of operation was undertaken because there had been a show-down at the check-point manned by the Green Berets or some other Muslim unit against a military column from Banja Luka or somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: So there was an operation, and since there were casualties --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It -- it -- it wasn't at the check-point at Kozarac. It was down the road at Jakupovici. And in -- and in -- and in response, the village of Kozarac gets shelled.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Okay. We don't have to be that precise. That road near Jakupovici -- Jakupovici is a hamlet that is part of the area that is called Kozarac. But it's less important. It is all related to Kozarac. It's only three kilometres from the centre of Kozarac. I know about that incident from hearsay, so please don't take it against me if I'm wrong about details.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So it's --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It doesn't mean that I don't want to tell the truth. There was this clash, there was the operation, and there were the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So let's not and -- let's not try and find the -- the people that may be involved in the incident in the hamlet of Jakupovici, but instead let's do a planned, co-ordinated, and sustained armed attack on a -- on a civilian settlement.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. It can remain as your allegation. Whether it was targeting civilians or the Green Berets, I don't know. I cannot believe that anybody would attack civilians just like that, but I'm not a direct participant of these events and I have no direct knowledge about it, so I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk about the cleansing of the Brdo in July 1992. In relation to that operation -- and the Brdo area being south of the town of Prijedor. In the -- in the operation to cleanse the non-Serbs, you had police information that the military police and the intervention platoon also took part in this operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there was talk about that. There was an operation to capture the people who, after the previous incident at Hambarine, had pulled out. All these settlements, Hambarine and Kurevo, all that is part of Brdo area, and I remember that people talked about this operation to catch the remaining assailants because the first operation was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In -- in paragraph 39 of your statement, you mention Fikret Kadiric, the former commander of the Prijedor police station. And you state that as you were going to work you saw two policemen putting him into a car, and you think that he was arrested at that point, and you said you didn't know where they were taking him or why. Now, I don't want you to recite the whole incident, but it's true, is it not, that you were actually there while the two men Batko Kovacevic -- or, Ranko Kovacevic, otherwise known as Batko, and Brane Cvijic arrested him, and you, in fact, went in the car with them to the -- to the police station. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, by the end of the year in 1992 during your two-day activities as a -- during your day-to-day activities as a police officer, you no longer saw Muslims in Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: You can't really say that because there were Muslims in Prijedor, they still in live in Prijedor, and they have always lived in Prijedor, at least as long as I've lived there. In the period you are talking about, I used to see very many Muslims in Prijedor. I was friends with them. I socialised with them. I helped them when they were too afraid to go out for a coffee. They asked me to join them to feel safer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, Mr. Reid said to you in your record of interview: "But from your day-to-day activities as a police officer, did you continue to see Muslims about in Prijedor?" And this is when he's talked about at the end of 1992. He actually asked you to estimate the number of Muslims in -- in -- in Opstina Prijedor, and you said that you didn't know the population. But he said: "From your day-to-day the activities, did you continue to see Muslims about in Prijedor?" You answered: "No, there were departures at that time. There were departures organised -- departures were organised with the Red Cross. It was no problem to see that. It was evident." And then Mr. Reid said: "And there were departures of Muslims from the Opstina?" And you said: "Yes." Mr. Reid said: "And why did those departures take place, do you know?" And you answered: "The people I talked to in my neighbourhood saw no chance for themselves. There were no future. They had no employment. Nothing. They were also not sure of their safety and the reasons were similar. Similar reasons were mentioned." Now, do you remember saying that in your record of interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, that's probably what I said, which is not inconsistent with my previous sentence. I did see Muslims in that time, but the fact is that they -- many of them sought ways to get out through the Red Cross to find a new life in the west. And people were afraid, they did not walk about town so much anymore. But it's not true that there were no Muslims at the time as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- my -- my time is up. I would seek leave to have an additional few minutes just to ask a couple of questions on one topic, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a few minutes, Your Honour. I -- I just need to ask a couple of questions on -- on two discrete topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you could conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in paragraph 10 of your statement, you mention that due to road communications, there had been -- communications had been disrupted, and the corridor was only opened at the end of June, and that this resulted in a loss of contract between CSB Banja Luka and the RS MUP. You're not a communications expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, I'm no expert in communication, but I know from my personal experience that I could not go anywhere further than Banja Luka or to the other side. I couldn't go farther than Novi Grad or Sanski Most. Do you mean these roads?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I could not, for instance, travel to Belgrade at the time. That's what I meant when I said that, but I'm really no expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But there was definitely communication between CSB Banja Luka and the RS MUP because this Trial Chamber has heard evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I draw Your Honours attention to P2743, paragraph 10, where the witness spoke and -- who was a communications expert and said there was always some way of communication, and Exhibit P2760, which is the 29th of June, 1992, RS MUP report for the period April to June 1992 where it states that the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. From time to time, I have the impression too much reference is made to distract the witness's attention. Why don't we just ask if witness whether there is a communication?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you're not aware, are you, that there was no communication between CSB Banja Luka -- that there was communication between CSB Banja Luka and the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, between Banja Luka and the RS? I don't know anything about that. I was only talking about the other kind of communication. From Prijedor you could go to Banja Luka. There were no obstacles. The telephones also worked from time to time when there was electricity, and police radio communications also worked when there was electricity. But power was more out than on at the time. Roads were not passable, not usable at the time. Whether some other communications were established, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Kvocka, you said in paragraph 73 of your statement that Drljaca was dismissed in 1993 for political reasons. You know, don't you, that he was appointed councillor of minister, that is councillor of the RS MUP minister, and a short time later he became the assistant to the RS MUP -- an assistant to the RS MUP, I should say better. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I'm aware that probably in 1993 there was some minor political turmoil, and Simo Drljaca was replaced as chief of the security station. I hear for the first time that he was named assistant minister, or advisor at the ministry at that time. I used to see him a lot at the time. I know that after the establishment of the security services centre, I don't know whether in 1994 or 1995, he was again appointed chief of the centre. That's what I know about Simo's movements at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, on page 55 it was said that it was an attack at a civilian populated centre. Was Kozarac completely demilitarised and was it a civilian area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: When I was talking about that attack, what you cited was probably the phrasing of the question, I know that Kozarac -- there was mention of an ultimatum at some point. There had been before that an ultimatum to surrender weapons. Kozarac had its own units and there were lists and I saw them in my trial, these lists, and there were lists of the members of the Green Berets and the Territorial Defence. There were photographs of dug-outs, trenches, underground pharmacies. So there was an armed force, a big force or a small force or a medium sized force, I don't know, but there was some sort of force and there were Muslim policemen who had quit from earlier police stations. So there was an armed formation there. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested on pages 52 and 53 that these were not clashes but they were instead a unilateral attack by the army. Did Serbs suffer any losses during these attacks?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I was not a direct participant, but I know that there was talk that there had been some Serb soldiers wounded and members of the JNA, which still existed and which was with the drawing [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could 65 ter 17760 be shown to the witness. Maybe it's on the next page. I don't see it. 65 ter 17760. Yes. This looks more like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from the public security station Prijedor of 26 May. Help us, please. Does it say that Banja Luka is hereby informed that war operations are still underway in Prijedor, and there follows a description of enumeration of the settlements engulfed by this, Kozarac, Kozarusa, Kamicani, and Trnopolje, and it says three members were wounded and killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. This was sent to the chief -- to the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does Omarska exist at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, Omarska does not exist at this moment. It was not established yet. Some people captured in these operations were arrested and a few days later Omarska was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph says that information exists about massacres and heinous murders of the innocent non-Muslim population. What is the non-Muslim population, Croats, Ukrainians?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there are Croats, Ukrainians, the Roma. There are Muslims, maybe some others. I don't really know, but it was mainly the Croats. Croats and Muslims were the non-Serbs in Prijedor and the rest were a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now look at the end of the third paragraph where it says that 168 people have been captured, and about 700 refugees have been provided for, and the moping up has been carried out in about 70 per cent of the territory. As a policeman, what's the different between 160 who have been captured and 700 who have been provided for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The 168 were captured in combat, and about the 700, I can say that they were probably the civilians who arrived in front of the sports hall in Prijedor. Even my wife took there and brought back a woman and a couple of children to our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And further down, you can see that 6 00 various weapons have been seized, and so on and so forth. Can you please tell us, during the conflict which started on the 24th in Kozarac, where did the civilians from Kozarac go to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I know that they arrived in front of the sports hall at first of their own initiative or with somebody's help. And then I believe that a majority of them went to Trnopolje. Most of the civilians went on their own to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you account for the fact that the Muslims civilians fled to Prijedor from the area of combat operations? Who controlled Prijedor at the time? Who was in power in the town that they arrived in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The power had been taken over by the Serbs, as it were, or the Serbian Democratic Party. I don't know how to formulate that. However, on the 30th of April, the power had been taken over which means that it was a month before the Serbs took power in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the civilians, including the 700 and those from Kozarac, fled the area of combat activities and sought refuge with the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, they did arrive and we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4220, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please be asked to slow down and make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the police towards the paramilitaries? Did the Serbian side have paramilitaries in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: We can say that there were renegades, those who were not under the regular police and military formations. There were individuals or minor groups possibly, and the attitude was such that they were in constant conflict, one could say. I believe that some were processed by the military bodies. I believe that there were various activities in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the Serbs who were in possession of illegal weapons or traded in illegal weapons? How were they treated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although there is no objection from the Prosecution, but I'm not sure whether this issue was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And neither was the issue of paramilitaries, and I let that one go, but not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 51 of today's transcript, it was claimed that it was suggested that only the non-Serb population was asked to hand over weapons, and the witness was asked whether such an appeal was also sent to the Serbs. What I'm trying to establish here is whether that implied a legally owned or illegally owned weapons, and if the Serbs were in possession of illegal weapons, how were they treated? I believe that this was a subject of the cross-examination. In more general terms, Mr. Kvocka, can you tell us why were Serbs detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: First of all, when we were talking about appeals to hand over weapons, it was not about the surrender of weapons but there were Serbs who were involved in the illegal trade of weapons and they were arrested. And not only those who -- that I mentioned before who were detained in Omarska for the lack of a better place to put them. There was a woman and two men who were detained there while I was there. I don't know about what happened later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the witness please be shown D1841.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did both Muslims and Serbs respond to the call-ups by the Territorial Defence and the army in equal measures? Or better say, who had militaries and who had paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In very general terms, the Muslim military were paramilitaries, and the Serbian army was a legal army, if we look at that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now would you please look at this report which was drafted on the 18th of May, 1992, and could you please tell us something about the claims with regard to the existence of armed units in Ljubija, Donja Ljubija, Carakovo, Kozarac, and Kozarusa. How does that information tally with what you know and what was the reason for which those groups were being asked to disarm?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The local communes which had majority Croat or Muslims populations had their organised military units which were not legal. That's why it was, as Madam Prosecutor called it -- an ultimatum was issued to surrender the weapons. The weapons were then seized. There were individuals who surrendered their weapons. I remember some of the details of the surrender of weapons in town more than in the villages, because the villages did not surrender weapons easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to the people who surrendered their weapons voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: They were issued with a receipt for the weapons that were stored in the building of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were also questions about the authorities or, rather, the police and their attitude towards those who broke law or breached discipline.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 18296. I'm afraid that we don't have a translation but we will ask the witness to help us with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Karadzic would like to put a question to the witness before the document's being brought up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I already did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the official police, and you are a professional policeman, towards the police officers who did not comply with the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The official position was always the same, and that is that no breaches of discipline were allowed with regard to the rules of service. That was the main position that always permeated all the discussions and it was always repeated and reiterated to the new recruits who had joined the police without a particular training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 18296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we see that document, could you not put some more specific questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can put it, did the police structures allow breaches of discipline and violation of the rules of service of their members? What was the position with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe that no such thing was allowed, even during the times of turmoil. Some people were called to task, they were prosecuted, but I can't give you any of the details because I was not involved in any of those matters. To me, personally, nobody ever said that I should do something that was not good. It was always repeated that I should do things in accordance with the law and the rules that prevailed that were our own positive police rules and laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your question was whether the police structure allowed breaches of discipline and violation of the rules of service, et cetera, and the witness answered no. Why do we need for that document? I don't see the need or foundation to seek to put further documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, does that mean that there is no issue about the witness's credibility that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but I asked Mr. Karadzic to put some more specific question with respect to the forthcoming document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if he establishes that the authorities didn't have a policy of not tolerating these breaches and then he shows a document which shows what the policy was and ask him how this jives with his statement, what is wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, I understand your point, but why could Mr. Karadzic not put some more specifics that forms the content of the forthcoming document, where the witness can answer the question or not, and he may then put the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think we are both disadvantaged by the fact that the document isn't translated, so we don't know its exact contents. But from what I can see from the description of the document, the document appears to be a statement of the policy of the authorities. It seems like this is directly specific enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances, I will allow the accused to continue. But let us see. If you could advise in the future about the manner in which to proceed on the part of the Defence. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I have translations of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exactly. It's not -- it's not uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian version is in e-court. Can the Serbian version be displayed, 65 ter 18296. We don't need two Serbian versions. One will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the public security station in Prijedor on the 11th of May. It conveys what had happened in Banja Luka on the 6th of May at a meeting of the council of the security services centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will skip everything up to paragraph 9 where it says: "The workers who are involved in criminal and illegal activities in the public security stations, and if such people exist they will be excluded from work and they will be prosecuted."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his questions. Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need it? Yes, Mr. Karadzic, what was your last question after reading out this sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was probably speeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was: Did you know -- were you aware of this position of the leadership of the MUP in your region with regard to the criminal behaviour of MUP members?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I already started answering by saying that it was a well known position. I would like to say that that was said to us even before this conclusion was reached, even before the meeting where this was discussed took place. I believe that it was told us at our many meetings that those things should be identified, forbidden, prosecuted, and that any failures in the work of the police should be prevented, especially if members of the police were involved in criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the following page, paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have that in English, paragraph 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here when it comes to disarming in the territory of the public security station, you should not take any measures until further notice. Does this mean, Mr. Kvocka, that on the 11th of May your public security station was still not intent on carrying out any disarming?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it says so here. There were no activities on the ground with regard to disarming, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why and when did the need arise to carry out disarming?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: There were some incidents. There were attacks on police and army members, and that's when ultimatums ensued. That's the sequence of events as I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm positive that this is already an exhibit, and I'm just trying to locate the exhibit number. It's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But we are talking about first two pages, given that it contains several separate documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we temporarily assign Defence number for the first two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that we will no longer need the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you are saying that on the 11th of May, as we can see from the document, that there are no such intentions, and you're saying that the need to disarm people arose after the incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 18320.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a while ago you said that a lot of people did surrender their weapons and they didn't suffer any problems as a result of that. In what villages did the people surrender their weapons? What -- were those villages subsequently attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I know that most often it was people from urban areas who did that on an individual basis. Now, I'm not 100 per cent sure whether this village called Cela, I think, I think that they also handed over weapons in an organised way once this handover started. And I think that there weren't any conflicts -- actually, I know that. As far as the village of Cela is concerned, there weren't any attacks. There weren't any clashes. There was no war. There were no clashes between anyone. There weren't any people who got killed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please focus on this document, the 5th of July, 1992. This is Prijedor reporting to Banja Luka about the disarmament plan; namely, that after the incidents on the 22nd, et cetera, that there was a conflict. And it says here in paragraph 3 towards the end: "After the situation had calmed down, the police and military police carried out joint moping-up operations in Trnopolje, Suhi Brod, Cela, Gomjenica, Donja and Gornja Puharska. In the course of these operations, we wish to note that citizens collected weapons themselves and handed them over to the army and police." Now, these locations mentioned in paragraph 3, were they attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: These locations that were referred to here were not attacked at all. Even without this document, I knew about Cela, and I didn't even think of Gomjenica. There are two Gomjenicas, a Serb Gomjenica and a Muslim Gomjenica. And there is Gornja Puharska too, and now I see that there weren't any armed conflicts there and also that there was no disarmament or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we see a list here of all the things that were handed over, and then here in number 7 it says: "Our station's records regarding seized and collected weapons and ammunition are as follows:" So what was the total number of villages around Prijedor that were at war? We see here that some were not at war at all. Now how many were at war against the Serbs? Can you refer to them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think it was only the area of Kozarac and the area of Brdo. These are two or three villages. I cannot say exactly. Hambarine. There is this other village there that is part of this Brdo. These other areas, I am not aware of any conflicts anywhere in the other Muslim villages; that is to say, only Kozarac and the area of Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We were talking about whether these were attacks or conflicts, so I would -- so on the Serb side, were there any casualties and if so when? Individually or whatever. For example, can you recall any colleagues of yours from the police force that fell victim?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well now given the time distance and without any documents, it's a bit difficult. I know that during the attack against Prijedor, by the Muslim army, I mean, there were quite a few Serb casualties and they were all members of the police force at the time. It was 18, 19, I cannot say exactly. Probably somewhere there are lists of fatalities. These were people who worked on securing various facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D16017, but we do not have it in e-court. So could the Serbian version be shown on the ELMO first and then the English version. The Serb version can actually be given to the witness, a hard copy, and the English version can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how this arose from the line of cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Prosecution suggested that these were one-sided attacks against civilian areas, and the witness said that these were clashes, conflicts, and now let us see when the first Serbs fell victim. And this has to do with policemen only now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe a bit later there were some other combatants. However, could this please be shown now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read it out, please, Radenko?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Djapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know this? Do you know of this case that the Serb policeman, Djapa, was killed on the 30th of April and then another one on the 9th and then another one on the 24th? Do you know of these cases?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I know these colleagues personally, most of them. And the cases are well known, too. Radenko Djapa was the first casualty after the Serb government was established.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Show me another part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we see the casualties here on the 24th, the 25th, 26th of May, and the 30th of May. Do you know all these people and do you know that all these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know. It was individual until the 30th of May, as I said, and then during this one night, the 30th of May, there were 17 victims. All of them were members of the active or reserve police force that were in charge of securing certain facilities during the course of that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was the 30th of May, then the 1st of June, the 4th of June. Do you know of all those cases?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, those are the deaths that occurred during that time, the people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of these cases? And this goes up to the 17th of June. There is a third page there, too.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I have all of this until the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The ones that you can see here up until the 17th of June, are you aware of all those cases?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about these cases, do you know of them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Radenko Grbic, Drago Aleksic, yes, yes, all of these people got killed by the remaining members of the unit in Kozarac that was not involved in Kozarac. They appeared on the approaches to the road after that. That's what I seem to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So from the 22nd of May until the 20th of June, over 50 persons got killed; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: When we add all of this up in terms of locations and dates, I haven't actually done the counting, but I just know for that one night between the 18th and 19th, as I've already mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We did not hear the question put by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, if you could put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Percentage-wise, how much is that -- or, rather, in terms of proportion, you don't have to give the exact percentage. In terms of proportion, how big is that as far as the police is concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's hard for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause. You just start answering the question while we are hearing the interpretation of Mr. Karadzic's question. Yes, could you answer the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It is hard for me to tell you what the percentages are 100 per cent sure, because I don't know the actual numbers for the reserve police if you put all the areas together, but it must be 10 per cent taking into account the entire police force in the entire region of Prijedor and the surrounding police stations. When you put all of that together, then it's perhaps even more than 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvocka, what is your view of that since this is not the front line. This is our territory in depth. What is your view of these losses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, what is my view? It is terrifying. It's not right. These people were killed by illegal forces. Well, then there is this other group. When there was this attack against Prijedor, it was an attempt made by Muslim units to take the town itself; whereas the rest, these were individual cases, a kind of terrorism. I don't know how to define it now. Radenko Djapa, the first one who was killed, he was shot in the street. It is a classical act of terrorism. Or these other people from Kozarac who were killed, their tractor was seized from them and they were set on fire. I cannot remember all the details now. I could be reminded. So there were a lot of acts of terrorism. And it would not be right not to take a view on this, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification -- oh, I'm sorry. Yes it's -- we have it in English as well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were also asked about departures, about people leaving. Was it only Muslims and Croats that were leaving or did Serbs leave too? And when did the population start leaving the municipality of Prijedor? Before the war did people leave?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, there were individual departures before the war, too, because in Bosnia from 1990 onwards there was some turbulence, political turbulence. So people who were thinking along those lines, they could assume that there might be some conflicts and then on an individual basis people would leave. People left before the conflict, both one and the other as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The police, the members of the Prijedor police, did they expel Muslims from Prijedor? Did they actively expel them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I don't have that impression. That's not what I feel, that they were involved in some kind of actively expulsion or that some kind of measures of coercion were taken forcing people to leave. I did not hear of that, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 18427. The number is right. Excellencies, can we go on for another five minutes or so? We started late anyway. And then I will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 5th of July. Again, could you please take a look at this. At the time, were there this many refugees from Croatia and is it correct? How does this fit into your own experience, these arrivals and departures?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see what this is all about. These are Serbs who were from other republics where there already was a conflict, and then they were coming into Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us this: Sometimes we have a problem with language, here. There was pressure to leave. Was it the authorities that were exerting pressure against the non-Serbs to leave, or was it the other way around? Was it the non-Serbs and even Serbs who were exerting pressure vis-a-vis the government to let them leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I've already said that I could not observe any methods that the government used to force Serbs or non-Serbs to leave. They probably wouldn't want to expel the Serbs. But I know from my own experience, my family is of mixed ethnicity, so I know relatives of my wife who asked for this. There were cases in the collection centre in Trnopolje. They dealt with some kind of organised departures abroad through the Red Cross. People would come at their own initiative. Even some who had no transportation from Prijedor, they would walk to Trnopolje, spend a few days there, and then the International Red Cross would write their names down and then they could leave. It is hard to go into the reasons and motives, if that's what you meant. People did not feel safe. There were conflicts throughout the former Yugoslavia. They were already there. Or there were conflicts in the making. In Croatia and Slovenia, there was a conflicts already going on, so I cannot go into the reasons and modifies. But I never read or heard that someone said in any proclamation or in any other document that all non-Serbs would have to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4224 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned during the cross-examination that you were not satisfied with the behaviour of the special detachment of the police from Banja Luka that came to help. What was the position of Mejakic and others with regard to this detachment and do you know what the position was of the centre of security services from Banja Luka vis-a-vis that detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: We, the local policemen who worked there, had certain problems with them and we were not satisfied. They were there for only a few days and we tried to deal with the situation as much as we could. Zeljko talked to Simo Drljaca in order to have that unit be withdrawn from the area, and eventually that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the security services centre in Banja Luka took into account Mr. Mejakic's intervention?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe that I was present when the order came for them to withdraw urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they members of the active police force? Were they professional policemen? What were their composition?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: They came from elsewhere, so I can't be sure. However, judging by their conduct and behaviour and the way they treated people, I'm sure that none of them were professional police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear how they behaved when they were not in the camp, when they were in other places?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I didn't know much about that. The only thing I knew was that that unit was very quickly disbanded. Somebody from Banja Luka told us that and we were satisfied, and we thought that we were also contributors to that success.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 5505.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention. The date is 24 June, immediately after their stay in Omarska. The public security station is asking the security services centre something, or rather they report the special detachment as behaving badly, they provide example, and they ask Mr. Zupljanin to take measures. Some names are mentioned here; right? Can you please look at the first and second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Zoran Janjetovic, who was mentioned in the second paragraph? He was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, I can't remember whether I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: He is a Serb. I'm sure that he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, he could be a Croat judging by the name, but I believe that he is a Serb, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can you look at the last photograph where Mr. Tutus writes to Mr. Zupljanin, and he says: "We firmly believe in your determination to have the service function in accordance with the rules on the work of organs of the interior ...," and so on and so forth, "we sincerely hope you will undertake measures which fall under your jurisprudence and that such unwelcome situations will disappear in the near future." Did they disappear?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe so, to a large extent. I am not aware of any subsequent incidents. When it comes to that unit, I learned that it was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't know that but we need to rise right now. We'll continue -- Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted? Perhaps I -- I need another five minutes, but I can take those after the break. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue after the break. We'll resume at half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Well, before that, I just wanted to tell you that we are sitting for the remainder of the session without Judge Lattanzi pursuant to Rule 15 bis. She cannot be with us due to her urgent personal matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, in fact, this document has not received a number. Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you were asked about a brawl, a fist-fight, or rather, beating of prisoners. Was it a rule or an exception, the beatings of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe I've already answered that those were individual incidents that occurred. We can't say they didn't happen. But it was far from being the rule or a regular situation, and I'm talking all the time about the period when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us out of the 2.500 people who were there, how many were beaten in total?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That's difficult to say now. I told you, I know about some individual incidents and some reports about some other people. It could be perhaps ten people who were beaten apart from the individual incidents that I could describe in greater detail. Perhaps not more than ten people were beaten, or at least I had the impression they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Kvocka, are you saying that not more than ten people were beaten out of 2.500 detainees at the time? Is it what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's what I said. It was my impression that another ten people were beaten in addition to the incidents that I've described in detail during my time at the camp and my entire tenure at the investigating centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And is that consistent with what you heard during your trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, during my trial I heard that after I left some more incidents occurred and more people were beaten, at least according to the evidence presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what is the truth as far as you know, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot make any judgements about what is true -- what was true after I left. I am talking only about the time when I was there and what I know. Maybe what I know is also not precise. Maybe more people were beaten, but I don't know about that. I didn't have the impression that it was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then where did that less than ten people come at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you cannot make any judgement at the moment, on what basis could you say that less than ten people were beaten at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I had the impression during the time I was there from the stories, from the talk among the prisoners and the guards. I had the impression that there were about ten cases of people beaten or somehow physically abused. That was my knowledge while I was there. Plus, the individual incidents I've described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You formed that impression based on what, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of my personal observations of peoples' injuries, or somebody said that someone else had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Concerning the beating of Mr. Civac, who was a member of the police force, you said that it was a matter of personal or professional revenge. Could you tell us something about the motives of those who beat him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It's difficult to talk about their real motives. They probably saw him as a work colleague, a former work colleague who suddenly found himself on the other side. Some earlier incidents occurred because the assailant's relatives had been killed in the conflict. It's difficult to judge the motives now, but these could have been some of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript did not mention that it was a kind of revenge, which was unacceptable but it could be a motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I said revenge in any case is not acceptable. But looking at these incidents, some possible motives are if a work colleague or a member of your family is killed, then a guard could try to take revenge in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, out of the guards, how many were inclined to such behaviour? You don't have to tell us the names. Just tell me the number.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Two or three guards all in all. Two or three guards acted that way. I cannot remember the names now. It would not be a problem for me to mention them, but I can't remember now. But the figure was two or three guards who deviated from their regular work procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was it viewed by the shift leaders, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe they tried to prevent this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 17 of today's transcript and related to paragraph 72 of your statement, it says Mr. Gruban told you about one of your brothers-in-law. He was concerned that he might fall into the category going to Manjaca. Tell me, on what did it depend whether somebody would go to Manjaca or released to go home?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: From what I knew while working at the investigating centre, these categories were decided depending on whether the people concerned were some sort of aiders and abetters or direct participants in the conflict or were not involved at all. So I found out later about one of my brothers-in-law, that he found into the category of aider and abetter. So he fell into a category that would not be released after the centre was disbanded but that he would be sent to Manjaca. But through some of his own connections he managed to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 51, the question suggested that civilians were detained in Omarska. Tell the Chamber, please, under what circumstances can a civilian be considered to have violated the law? Were they detained as civilians or was there some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm concerned it's a pretty relative thing. If you judge by the way they were dressed, many of them looked like civilians. However, the investigations showed that they had taken part in the conflict. Many of them had weapons that were taken away from them during capture. So this term "civilian" is very relative, although some people used it. Those who were released later were partly civilians and they were captured together with others. Maybe there was a small number of people like that, but I cannot judge about that because I was not involved in the investigations. But you cannot apply to them generally the term "civilians" because you can mount an armed insurgency while wearing civilian clothes. So under certain circumstances even a civilian can become a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Kvocka: Generally speaking, did you have any knowledge about my personal views concerning respect for the law, the rules of warfare, humanitarian law, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I can remember that many times on television and in the press, although the press was not always available, there were statements on many occasions that international humanitarian organisations have to be respected, prisoners of war have to be respected, as well as civilian population in towns, and I believe some specific orders were even issued by you or by the MUP. But according to your public statements, your view was that international conventions and morale principles and principles of human dignity have to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kvocka, for testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During your cross-examination, Mr. Kvocka, it's transcript page 32, you said, I quote: "I think that it would not be fair on my behalf to say to the Defence team," I mean Mr. Karadzic's Defence team, "what I heard during the trial which took place in 2001." So could you explain to us why it would not be fair on your part to tell the Karadzic team that you -- the things that you came to know during your trial?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I've already forgotten what events were meant in the question, but what I wanted to say was that the investigator who contacted me wanted to know about my direct knowledge and all these other things that I learned later. Perhaps I didn't even think of it, but I cannot claim with any certainty that something I heard here is necessarily true. Those were the reasons that I had in mind when I thought about this. I focused only on what I personally observed, heard, saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Kvocka. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thank you, too, and I'm glad if I managed to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it the next witness is ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's Dragan Radetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, are you going to cover Mr. Radetic, the next one? Could you explain to us why Rule 90(E) advice is warranted with respect to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Because the witness worked in the investigative centre at Keraterm and also because he was a military prosecutor or deputy military prosecutor subsequent to his duties in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radetic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Thank you. I take it you know this very well, but before you commence your evidence, Mr. Radetic, I must draw your attention to a rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Radetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Radetic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am one of those people who speak very fast, but I have to ask you to mind the rhythm and leave a pause between question and answer so we don't have to repeat things for the transcript. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9660 is the document I would like to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the left side of the screen, please. Now we see both versions of your statement.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the last page so the witness can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
